title: Social Justice in Islam
description:
This course explores the comprehensive framework of social justice in Islam, examining how the Quran and Sunnah establish principles of equity, charity, and compassion for the vulnerable. Students will learn about justice (adl) as a divine attribute and its manifestation in Islamic law and practice.

The course covers Quranic commands for justice, the importance of standing against oppression, the institution of charity (zakat and sadaqah), and the specific rights of orphans, refugees, and the poor. Classical scholars' interpretations are connected to modern social justice movements.

Participants will understand that Islam does not separate spiritual worship from social responsibility, and that true faith requires active engagement in creating just societies. The course provides both theoretical foundations and practical guidance for Muslims committed to social justice.
short_description: Explore Islam's comprehensive framework for social justice, equity, and compassion

modules.title: Justice in the Quran
modules.description: Examining the Quranic foundation for social justice

lessons.title: Quranic Commands for Justice
lessons.content:
The Quran establishes justice (adl) as a fundamental divine attribute and a command for all believers. Allah says: 'O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives.' (4:135). This verse commands absolute commitment to justice, even when it is personally difficult.

Another foundational verse states: 'O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.' (5:8). This verse specifically addresses the challenge of being fair to those we dislike.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir, explains that these verses were revealed regarding the early Muslim community's disputes, establishing that justice must prevail over personal interests, tribal loyalties, or emotional biases. Justice is not optional but a requirement of faith.

Imam Al-Tabari adds that 'standing firm' (qawamun) implies active effort, not passive acceptance. Muslims must actively pursue justice in their personal lives, communities, and societies, working to establish systems that protect the rights of all people.

lessons.title: Justice as a Divine Attribute
lessons.content:
Justice is not merely a human obligation in Islam but a reflection of Allah's own nature. The Quran states: 'Indeed, Allah commands justice, good conduct, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, bad conduct, and oppression.' (16:90). This comprehensive verse links justice with all forms of righteousness.

Imam Al-Ash'ari, the founder of the Ash'ari school of theology, explained that Allah's actions are all characterized by wisdom and justice. When Allah commands justice, He is asking humans to reflect His divine attribute in their conduct.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Be just, for justice is nearest to piety.' (Sunan Abu Dawud, 4885). This hadith establishes that justice is not separate from worship but integral to it. A person cannot claim piety while being unjust.

This understanding means that social justice is not a modern addition to Islam but part of its core message. The Quran's emphasis on justice permeates its legislation, from inheritance laws to criminal justice to economic fairness, creating a comprehensive system for just societies.

modules.title: Standing Against Oppression
modules.description: The Islamic obligation to oppose injustice and support the oppressed

lessons.title: The Prohibition of Oppression (Zulm)
lessons.content:
Oppression (zulm) is one of the gravest sins in Islam, with severe warnings in both the Quran and Hadith. Allah says: 'And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare in horror.' (14:42). This verse warns that oppression will be fully accounted for.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Beware of oppression, for oppression will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection.' (Sahih Muslim, 2578). This hadith illustrates that oppression creates lasting consequences beyond this world.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah in 'Majmu' al-Fatawa' distinguishes between types of zulm: oppressing Allah by associating partners with Him, oppressing others through injustice, and oppressing oneself through sin. All forms are prohibited, but the most condemnable is oppressing fellow human beings.

Islam's prohibition of oppression is comprehensive, covering economic exploitation, political tyranny, social discrimination, and personal wrongs. The Quran addresses specific forms of oppression, including exploitation of workers (93:9-11), neglect of orphans' rights (4:2-6), and corruption in public life (11:85).

lessons.title: Speaking Truth to Power
lessons.content:
Islam commands Muslims to speak truthfully and to stand against injustice, even when it is dangerous. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The best jihad (struggle) is a word of truth in the presence of a tyrannical ruler.' (Sunan Abu Dawud, 4344). This hadith establishes that speaking truth to power is among the highest forms of religious struggle.

The Quran supports this principle: 'O you who have believed, fear Allah and be among those who are true.' (9:119). Truthfulness (sidq) requires honesty in all circumstances, including when addressing those in authority.

Imam Al-Nawawi in 'Riyadh al-Salihin' explains that speaking truth to power requires wisdom, not recklessness. The goal is to correct injustice, not to create more chaos. This wisdom includes timing, manner, and understanding the political context.

Historical examples include Bilal ibn Rabah's steadfastness against persecution, Abu Bakr's honesty in all matters, and Umar ibn al-Khattab's accountability to the public. These examples show that Islamic leadership requires being answerable to the community, not above it.

modules.title: Charity and Economic Justice
modules.description: Zakat, sadaqah, and the Islamic system for economic fairness

lessons.title: Zakat: The Pillar of Economic Justice
lessons.content:
Zakat (زكاة) is the third pillar of Islam, obligatory on all Muslims who meet the minimum wealth threshold (nisab). The Quran commands: 'And establish prayer and give zakat, and whatever good you put forward for yourselves - you will find it with Allah.' (2:110). This establishes zakat as a fundamental religious duty.

The purpose of zakat is not merely charity but economic justice. By requiring the wealthy to give 2.5% of their accumulated wealth annually to specific categories of recipients ( Quran 9:60), Islam creates a systematic redistribution of wealth that prevents extreme poverty.

Imam Al-Nawawi, in his book 'al-Majmu',' explains that zakat purifies wealth and soul. The wealthy are reminded that their fortune is a trust from Allah, not solely their own earning. The poor receive their right, not charity.

Zakat institutions have historically functioned as social safety nets, providing for the poor, freeing debtors, and funding community development. In modern contexts, effective zakat collection and distribution can address poverty, fund education, and support economic development in Muslim communities worldwide.

lessons.title: Sadaqah and Voluntary Charity
lessons.content:
Beyond the obligatory zakat, Islam encourages voluntary charity (sadaqah) in numerous verses and hadith. The Quran states: 'The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed which grows seven ears; in each ear is a hundred grains.' (2:261). This metaphor illustrates the multiplied reward for charity.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Charity does not decrease wealth.' (Sahih Muslim, 2588). This seemingly paradoxical statement reflects the spiritual and social benefits that come from generosity, which often manifest in material blessings as well.

Imam Al-Ghazali in 'Ihya Ulum al-Din' categorizes charity into levels, from the minimum of smiling at someone to the highest of helping others become self-sufficient. This hierarchy shows that charity encompasses all forms of goodness.

Modern applications of sadaqah include: supporting education, funding medical care, building clean water projects, and providing microfinance for small businesses. The principle of sadaqah jariyah (ongoing charity) encourages sustainable giving that continues to benefit recipients long after the initial donation.

modules.title: Protecting the Vulnerable
modules.description: Islamic rights of orphans, refugees, and the marginalized

lessons.title: Rights of Orphans in Islam
lessons.content:
Islam places tremendous emphasis on the care of orphans (yatama), with severe warnings for those who neglect them. The Quran dedicates an entire surah to the topic (Surah Al-Duha, 93:9) and commands: 'As for the orphan, do not oppress him.' (93:9). This brief but powerful command establishes the absolute prohibition of wronging orphans.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be like these two in Paradise,' indicating with his index and middle fingers. (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5304). This hadith shows that caring for orphans is among the most beloved deeds to Allah.

Imam Ibn Kathir explains in his tafsir that the Quran's concern for orphans reflects their extreme vulnerability. Without parents, they are easily exploited, their inheritance stolen, and their rights ignored. Islam provides legal protections and encourages community support.

Practical applications include: sponsoring orphans through reputable organizations, supporting foster care systems, ensuring orphans receive their full inheritance, and providing emotional support. The Quran specifies that orphans' wealth should be managed carefully and returned to them when they reach maturity (4:6).

lessons.title: Caring for Refugees and Displaced People
lessons.content:
The Islamic tradition has deep roots in caring for refugees and displaced people, as the early Muslim community itself experienced displacement. The Muhajirun fled persecution in Makkah and were welcomed in Madinah, establishing the principle of hospitality to those fleeing oppression.

The Quran commands: 'And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then deliver him to his place of safety.' (9:6). This verse establishes the obligation to protect refugees, even from hostile groups.

Imam Al-Shafi'i and other jurists developed comprehensive rulings on the rights of refugees (musta'min), including protection from harm, access to basic needs, and the right to practice their faith. These rulings demonstrate Islam's proactive stance on refugee protection.

Modern applications include: supporting refugee resettlement organizations, providing emergency relief, advocating for refugee rights, and creating welcoming communities for displaced Muslims and non-Muslims alike. The Prophet's example of welcoming refugees to Madinah provides a timeless model.
